checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: Scraped prices are noisy. A product briefly shows $3 instead of $300.

options.label: Store every sample
options.verdict: One malformed page fires alerts to every watcher and poisons the price history chart. Scrapers see broken markup, A/B tests and regional currencies — treating every sample as truth guarantees false alarms.

options.label: Validate against recent history
options.verdict: A sample far below the 30-day minimum is more likely a parse error than a real price. Quarantine it, confirm with a re-scrape, and only then accept it.

options.label: A genuine flash sale is delayed by verification
A re-scrape path for suspicious samples
A threshold that will sometimes be wrong
The need to store fewer samples

defend.explain: You store more, not less — the quarantined ones too, since a repeated 'implausible' price is how you learn the threshold is wrong. The cost is latency on real drops and a heuristic that needs tuning.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder
checkpoints.prompt: ~500M products in the catalogue, ~1M extension users.

choices: Only watched products plus a popular tail
rungs.note: You track what someone cares about, not the whole catalogue.
Popular, volatile products earn more frequent scrapes.

checkpoints.explain: The catalogue is enormous but the working set is not. Prioritised scheduling is what keeps a 500M-product problem tractable.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the path from a scrape to a fired alert.
checkpoints.explain: Validation sits between scraping and storage so a bad sample never reaches history. Confirmed price changes are published to Kafka, and the alert matcher fans out to watchers. Notifications are the terminal step, deliberately after the price is trusted.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: A flash sale ended an hour ago. Alerts for it are still being delivered.
checkpoints.explain: The alert matcher is 6M events behind, so it is working through price changes from an hour ago and dutifully notifying people about a sale that has ended. Alerts are inherently time-sensitive: the consumer needs to scale with watcher fan-out, and events should carry an expiry so stale ones are dropped rather than delivered.

wrong.Notification Service: Delivering promptly — the events it receives are simply old.
wrong.Validation: A 4% quarantine rate is normal and unrelated to timing.
wrong.Scraper Pool: Scraping is healthy; the delay is entirely downstream.
